title: Problem-Solving: Take the Lead
hook: Payroll cells can make a rushed fix look like progress.
counterintuition: A prescribed answer often creates quiet resistance; lead the process so both people help shape a usable next step.
tryThisNow: Before offering a fix, list three possible options and one standard both sides would accept before seeing the options.
keyTakeaway: Move into problem-solving only after enough understanding and expression, then lead joint inquiry through options, standards, and specific agency-matched commitments.

breakdown.fastRead:
The payroll sheet sits beside an empty job description. Olivia feels two real pressures at once: burnout is rising, and the business may not be ready for a full-time hire.

To lead well, protect the process from drift. Do not grab the answer alone. Name a stage shift: make options first, choose shared standards, then end with steps each partner can truly control.
breakdown.deepRead:
Olivia could win the first-hire argument and still lose the business. If she pushes one answer too early, her partner will evaluate that answer instead of helping design the right one. If nobody leads, the conversation will feel meaningful and end with nothing more than relief.

Problem-solving is a stage shift. It belongs after people have heard each other and said what matters. When it arrives too early, fixing becomes a way to escape understanding. When it arrives too late or not at all, the conversation drifts. The skill is to notice when the question has changed from "what is happening between us?" to "what should we do now?"

Leading means keeping the process from wandering, not taking control away from them.

At this stage, joint inquiry into solutions starts with the process, not the answer. "I can think of one path, but I want us to generate a few before we judge them. What would you add?" That sentence keeps ownership shared. A contractor, a cautious full-time hire, and a deferred hire tied to a revenue trigger can all be on the table before either partner attacks or defends the first idea.

Then choose standards before choosing winners. What would both people call responsible? Cash runway, customer response time, founder sleep, training capacity, service quality. A mutual standard keeps the discussion from collapsing into my preference against yours. After that, build on proposals. Start with the useful part of the other person's idea, adjust the risky part, and keep moving toward a design.

Specificity is the bridge between insight and behavior. "We'll figure it out" is not a plan. "You draft the contractor job description by Thursday, I update the payroll model by Friday, and we decide after next week's revenue report" is a plan.
breakdown.fullRead:
Maja hears the relief in the room as soon as the student organization stops arguing about the failed event plan. People understand each other better. The permit form is still blank. The campus room calendar is filling, and the task board has three cards labeled "someone." That is the moment drift begins.

A good conversation can fail at the end because nobody leads the stage shift. Everyone feels that something has been aired. Nobody wants to spoil the relief by asking who will do what. Two days later, the same vague hope returns as a deadline problem. Problem-solving is not less human than listening. It is how the listening becomes behavior when behavior is needed.

The opposite failure is unilateral prescription. One person arrives with a solution, gets exhausted agreement, and mistakes silence for buy-in. The plan later fails because the other person never helped design it or never had control over the promised piece. Stronger pressure will not fix that. Better process will.

Ask: are we ready to design, or are we using design to avoid something unfinished? If the hurt has not been heard, the solution may feel like a lid. If the feelings have been acknowledged and the shared problem is clear, design can begin. That order matters.

Taking the lead means keeping the work from drifting, not grabbing the steering wheel from the other person. The lead can say, "Let's make three options before we evaluate any of them." The lead can ask, "What standard would we both trust before we know which option wins?" The lead can build: "The part I like in your idea is the earlier deadline. The part that worries me is who has authority to approve it. What if we pair your deadline with my approval route?"

Agency is the hard test. A commitment is useful only when it matches what the person can actually control. Aman may be sitting in a faculty committee while the minutes document is projected on the screen. If senior faculty push him to promise a course roster change he cannot approve, the specific next step is theater. A better commitment would be, "I can draft the impact note by Tuesday and send it to the chair before the email deadline. I cannot guarantee the roster change alone." That is not evasion. It is honest problem-solving.

Standards protect the conversation from preferences disguised as principles. Diego and his partner may disagree about quiet hours, but both might accept standards such as sleep before early shifts, lease rules, notice before guests, and a decibel limit after 10 p.m. Once the standards are named, the rule is not simply his way or their way. It is a design against agreed criteria.

Specific next steps turn insight into behavior. Vincent can turn neighborhood resentment into a snow-removal rota only when names, sidewalks, and the first storm date appear on the block map. Jack can improve a hospital discharge handoff only when pharmacy, nursing, and discharge planning each name the part they control. The next step should be visible enough that everyone knows whether it happened.

Some conversations should not solve yet. They end best with understanding, apology, or expression because design would be premature. But when action is needed, do not leave with warmth alone. Warmth does not clear a sidewalk, file a permit, call a patient, or hire the first employee. A shared next step does.

examples.title: Olivia Lists Options Before Judgment

planSpec.audience: partners ready to move from understanding to design
planSpec.stakes: burnout and payroll risk both have real claims
planSpec.requiredBeat: Olivia proposes three options before either partner evaluates the first one

examples.scenario: A payroll spreadsheet glows beside an empty job description while the revenue trigger sits in a yellow cell. Olivia must decide whether to pitch her preferred first hire. Instead she proposes three options before evaluation: contractor, cautious full-time hire, or deferred hire tied to revenue.
examples.whatToDo: Lead the process by generating options first. Olivia should keep both burnout and payroll risk visible before either partner attacks a single answer.
examples.whyItMatters: The first option often becomes a fight. Several options let the partners design instead of defend.

examples.title: Maja Ends with Owners

planSpec.audience: student leaders whose talk keeps ending in relief without action
planSpec.stakes: a campus event will fail if roles remain vague
planSpec.requiredBeat: Maja ends the meeting with owners and dates instead of 'we will figure it out'

examples.scenario: "So who owns the permit by Friday?" Maja asks, pointing from the permit form to the campus room calendar and task board. The group has finally understood why the last event stalled. Now Maja must decide whether to let relief end the meeting or name owners and dates before anyone closes a laptop.
examples.whatToDo: Convert relief into action. Maja should assign the permit, room confirmation, and task-board updates with dates before the meeting ends.
examples.whyItMatters: "We will figure it out" feels cooperative and changes nothing. Specific owners protect the event from drift.

examples.title: Diego Asks for Standards

planSpec.audience: housemates shifting from grievance to design
planSpec.stakes: sleep loss is turning affection into irritation
planSpec.requiredBeat: Diego asks for standards they would both accept before picking a rule

examples.scenario: It took Diego a week of watching the decibel app glow on the bedside table to stop making it his rule against theirs. The work shifts and apartment lease sit between them. Before picking quiet hours, they must decide which standards both would accept: sleep, notice, guests, and lease limits.
examples.whatToDo: Choose mutual standards before choosing the rule. Diego should ask what a fair quiet-hours agreement must protect for both people.
examples.whyItMatters: Standards move the problem away from my way versus your way. A rule built against shared criteria has a better chance of holding.

examples.title: Jack Builds on the Nurse's Proposal

planSpec.stakes: patients are getting duplicate calls and missed instructions
planSpec.requiredBeat: Jack builds on the nurse's proposal before naming the part pharmacy can actually control

examples.scenario: A discharge packet with two phone numbers lies under the call log while the pharmacy queue keeps moving. Jack must decide whether to take over the redesign. He builds on the nurse's proposal first, then names the part pharmacy can actually control: medication-call timing and escalation notes.
examples.whatToDo: Build on the proposal and match commitments to agency. Jack should contribute pharmacy's controllable piece without making himself owner of the whole discharge system.
examples.whyItMatters: Taking over would reduce shared ownership. A specific pharmacy commitment helps the handoff without pretending one role controls all variables.

examples.title: Aman Refuses the False Commitment

planSpec.stakes: a junior lecturer may agree to work they cannot control to end the meeting
planSpec.requiredBeat: Aman asks which commitments are actually his before the plan is recorded

examples.scenario: At 2:17 p.m., Aman watches the committee minutes document projected on a screen beside the course roster and email deadline. The chair begins recording him as owner of a workload change. He has to choose between closure and accuracy, so he asks which commitments are actually his before the plan is saved.
examples.whatToDo: Test agency before accepting the commitment. Aman can promise an impact note by Tuesday, but not a roster change he cannot approve.
examples.whyItMatters: A false commitment gives the room closure and gives the junior person a burden without power. Specificity only helps when control matches the promise.

examples.title: Vincent Turns Complaints into a Rota

planSpec.audience: neighbors turning recurring resentment into next steps
planSpec.stakes: elderly residents need predictable help before the next storm
planSpec.requiredBeat: Vincent turns three complaints into a rota with names, sidewalks, and first storm date

examples.scenario: You can see the laminated block map on the porch table, a snow shovel against the rail, and a weather alert for Thursday. Vincent does not let the postmortem end with goodwill. He turns three complaints into a rota with names, sidewalks, and the first storm date.
examples.whatToDo: Make the next step visible. Vincent should record who clears which sidewalk and when the rota starts before neighbors leave.
examples.whyItMatters: Community goodwill does not help elderly residents during the first storm. Names, sidewalks, and dates turn concern into behavior.

questions.prompt: Two business partners understand each other's concerns about burnout and payroll, then one immediately pushes a full-time hire. What problem-solving move is missing?
choices: Generate several options before evaluating the first one.
Return to feelings and avoid any design work.
Let the more exhausted partner decide alone.
questions.explanation: A single early option invites attack or defense. Several options let both partners design around burnout and payroll risk.

questions.prompt: A student event team leaves a meeting saying, "We will figure out the permit." The deadline is Friday and nobody owns it. What should the lead do?
choices: Trust the good energy from the meeting.
Name the owner, action, and deadline before the meeting ends.
Schedule another meeting to discuss how everyone feels.
questions.explanation: Good energy can drift. A specific next step turns the conversation into action: who files what by when.

questions.prompt: Housemates are arguing about quiet hours. One wants 10 p.m.; the other wants midnight. What is the best next move before choosing a time?
choices: Pick the earlier time because sleep matters more.
Average the two times and move on.
Agree on standards such as sleep, work shifts, notice, and lease limits.
questions.explanation: Standards give the rule a shared basis. Without them, the discussion stays trapped in preference against preference.

questions.prompt: A pharmacist in a discharge redesign meeting likes a nurse's proposal but sees a pharmacy constraint. Which response best builds on the proposal?
choices: Reject the proposal because it misses pharmacy's reality.
Name what works, then add the pharmacy-controlled timing and escalation piece.
Take ownership of the whole discharge process to simplify accountability.
questions.explanation: Building starts with the useful part, then adjusts the part pharmacy can control. Taking over would weaken shared ownership.

questions.prompt: A junior lecturer is asked to promise a course roster change he cannot approve. What makes the requested commitment weak?
choices: It is too specific for a committee setting.
It does not match the agency he actually has.
It would require sending an email.
questions.explanation: Specific commitments help only when the person controls the promised action. Otherwise the plan creates false closure.

questions.prompt: Neighbors spend twenty minutes agreeing that elderly residents need snow help, then nobody assigns sidewalks. Which failure mode is this?
choices: Drift after a meaningful conversation.
Unilateral prescription by one neighbor.
Too many mutual standards.
questions.explanation: The conversation created shared concern but no action. Drift is the failure to convert understanding into next steps when action is needed.

questions.prompt: A person offers a complete solution and asks, "Any objections?" The other person agrees quietly, then undermines the plan later. What likely happened?
choices: The solution was too collaborative.
The other person helped design too many options.
The lead used unilateral prescription instead of joint inquiry.
questions.explanation: Surface agreement is not ownership. Joint inquiry invites the other person to shape the answer before commitment.

questions.prompt: After a painful exchange, one person moves quickly to solutions before the other has expressed what happened. How should the stage shift be evaluated?
choices: It may be premature because fixing can avoid hearing.
It is always efficient to solve before feelings grow.
It proves the person has taken responsibility.
questions.explanation: Problem-solving belongs after enough understanding and expression. Used too early, it can become a lid on the conversation.

questions.prompt: After a planning meeting, two colleagues have three options and a shared standard written on the whiteboard, but no owner or date for the chosen action. What still must happen before the conversation becomes action?
choices: They should revisit every feeling once more.
They need specific next steps with owners and timing.
They should avoid commitments so nobody feels pressured.
questions.explanation: Options and standards are not behavior yet. Owners and timing make it clear what will happen and how everyone will know.

reviewCards.front: What is the difference between taking the lead and taking over?
reviewCards.back: Taking the lead protects the process: options, standards, and next steps. Taking over prescribes the answer and removes shared ownership.

reviewCards.front: Why generate options before judging the first one?
reviewCards.back: The first option can become a fight. Multiple options keep the conversation in design rather than defense.
They prevent the plan from becoming my preference against yours. Standards create criteria both people can trust.

reviewCards.front: What makes a next step real?
reviewCards.back: It has an owner, an action, and timing, and it matches what that person can actually control.
When it is used before enough listening and expression have happened, especially as a way to escape discomfort.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The core skill is leading the design process without stealing ownership of the solution from the other person.

ifThenPlans.plan: If you have one solution ready, then list two more options before either person evaluates any of them.
If the meeting ends with relief, then ask for owner, action, and date before people leave.
If preferences clash, then name mutual standards before choosing a rule.
If someone asks you to commit, then check whether the action is actually inside your control.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Within 24 hours, take one unresolved issue and write three options, one mutual standard, and one next step with owner and date.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, build on another person's proposal by naming what works in it before adding the constraint or adjustment you see.

memorableLines.text: Taking the lead means keeping the work from drifting, not grabbing the steering wheel from the other person.
Specificity is the bridge between insight and behavior.
A commitment is useful only when it matches what the person can actually control.
